Computers

A competent adult should be able to buy a computer, drive it, make documents with it, understand why it is slow, not lose their files, not get scammed, and not be afraid of it.

53 lessons for a seven-year-old and a nine-year-old, taught at a kitchen table with two Raspberry Pi 400s. Not a computer science course. Not an engineering course.

Each lesson is one page you scroll through together. Arrow keys move a slide at a time. Press N to stack the slides with the teacher notes underneath — that is how you read a lesson the night before.

0. What Is This Thing?

Begins with 'a computer is the thing on the desk' and ends with them speccing and pricing a machine for a stated job.

  • 01
    What Is a Computer?

    Point at any object and say whether it is a computer, naming its input, output, and storage.

  • 02
    Build the Four Boxes

    Draw the block diagram of any computer and point to each part on a real Pi 400.

  • 03
    The Peripheral Zoo

    Name every common port and cable and match them by sight.

  • 04
    Inside the Tower

    Identify PSU, motherboard, CPU, RAM, drive, and GPU in a real machine.

  • 05
    Reading a Spec Sheet

    Read a real computer listing and say which numbers matter for a stated job.

  • 06
    Build a Computer

    Spend a fixed budget on parts for a stated use case and defend every choice.

1. Driving the Machine

From 'where did my download go' to a filing system they designed and a repeatable procedure for when something breaks.

  • 07
    What an Operating System Is

    Explain what sits between you and the hardware, and shut down properly without being told.

  • 08
    Typing Bootcamp

    Find the home row without looking, and start a daily habit.

  • 09
    Where Your Stuff Lives

    Use the mouse deliberately, navigate the folder tree, copy, move, rename, and delete files, and build a folder structure for school subjects three levels deep.

  • 10
    Icons Lie, Extensions Tell the Truth

    Predict what will open a file from its extension, not its icon.

  • 11
    It's Broken - Now What?

    Run the troubleshooting procedure on an unfamiliar failure without panicking.

2. Making Things

The three office tools, each attached to something they chose. Ends with a real talk given to a real audience.

  • 12
    Plain Text and Word Processors

    Say what a word processor adds to plain text, and save vs save-as correctly.

  • 13
    Headings Beat Bold

    Format a document with real headings instead of making text big.

  • 14
    Long Documents

    Generate a table of contents, add page numbers, and find-and-replace across a document.

  • 15
    Project: The Report

    Produce a two-page illustrated report with title page, contents, headings, and page numbers.

  • 16
    Spreadsheets, Day One

    Say what a spreadsheet is for and enter data into a grid without fighting it.

  • 17
    The Equals Sign

    Write a formula, use SUM and AVERAGE, and fill down.

  • 18
    Sort, Filter, Chart

    Build a tracker for something they care about and chart it honestly.

  • 19
    Slides Support the Talker

    Build a slide deck that helps them talk instead of replacing them.

  • 20
    Present Day

    Give a three-minute talk with slides, and move a chart between three applications.

3. Everything Is Numbers

Every file they have made so far, re-explained as numbers. Ends with them compressing their own artwork by hand.

  • 21
    Only Two Things

    Explain why a computer uses only 0 and 1, count to 31 in binary on one hand, and predict the output of NOT, AND, OR, NAND and NOR.

  • 22
    Bits, Bytes, Gigabytes

    Estimate how many photos or songs fit on a given drive.

  • 23
    Bitmaps

    Compute the file size of a picture from its dimensions, with a pencil.

  • 24
    Color Is Three Numbers

    Predict a hex color code from an RGB mix, and read one in the wild.

  • 25
    Letters Are Numbers Too

    Encode and decode a message by hand and explain why emoji needed a bigger scheme.

  • 26
    Making It Smaller

    Compress their own pixel art by hand and say what lossy compression throws away.

  • 27
    Formats Are Containers

    Choose the right format to send something, and say what a proprietary format costs you.

4. Fast, Slow, and Forever

The mental model most adults never acquire. Ends with them diagnosing a slow machine and restoring a file they deleted on purpose.

  • 28
    The Desk and the Filing Cabinet

    Explain why unsaved work disappears when the power goes out.

  • 29
    The Speed Pyramid

    Order the storage hierarchy by speed and say what cache is for.

  • 30
    Why Is It Slow?

    Open a task manager, find the bottleneck, and name it.

  • 31
    Physical Media

    Explain how three different media physically store a bit.

  • 32
    From a Room to Your Wrist

    Put six generations of computer in order and say what got smaller and why it mattered.

  • 33
    How You Lose Everything

    Set up a real backup and restore a file they deleted on purpose.

  • 34
    The Cloud Is Someone Else's Computer

    Say the difference between sync, backup, and storage, and what happens offline.

5. The Command Line

The same filesystem from Unit 1, now in text. Ends with a script that does something they actually want done.

  • 35
    Why a Terminal Exists

    Navigate the filesystem in text and know where they are at all times.

  • 36
    Making and Breaking

    Create, copy, move and delete from the command line, carefully.

  • 37
    Reading and Writing

    Read a file, edit it, and check how much space things take.

  • 38
    Small Tools, Combined

    Chain commands with a pipe to answer a question about their own file.

  • 39
    Where Software Comes From

    Write a small script, install something with a package manager, and say why not to run a random download.

6. The Internet

From 'the internet is magic' to tracing a packet, reading a URL, and spotting a phish.

  • 40
    Driving a Browser

    Read a URL like a sentence and use tabs, history, and print-to-PDF deliberately.

  • 41
    What Happens When You Press Enter

    Trace the path from their keyboard to a server and back, out loud.

  • 42
    Searching, and Believing

    Refine a search with operators and say who wrote a page and who paid for it.

  • 43
    Why It's Free

    Explain how an ad-funded site makes money from their attention.

  • 44
    Scams

    Spot a phishing attempt and explain the house rule about codes and money.

  • 45
    Email and Footprints

    Send a proper email and say what is permanent and what is public.

7. Making the Machine Do Something

Enough programming to demystify it and to make Unit 3 concrete. Ends with code that moves atoms.

  • 46
    Telling It Exactly

    Build a program in Scratch with a loop that draws something.

  • 47
    If, and Remembering

    Use a conditional and a variable to make a small game with a score.

  • 48
    Python, in Words

    Write and run a program that asks a question and uses the answer.

  • 49
    Deciding and Repeating

    Write a guessing game with hints that ends when it should.

  • 50
    Doing It a Hundred Times

    Write a script that does a boring job to a whole folder at once.

  • 51
    Code That Moves Atoms

    Blink an LED from a program, and change how it blinks.

8. Capstone

Something real, built and documented and demoed.

  • 52
    Pitch and Build

    Write a one-page spec for something real and start building it.

  • 53
    Demo Night

    Demonstrate a finished thing to an audience, with written instructions someone else could follow.

4 of 53 lessons written. No accounts, no analytics, nothing tracked. Open any file in a browser — there is nothing to build. There is a space course too.
